source_refs.note: Exercise 11.3, Question 10: book page 296. The book prints no answers for Unit 11.

blocks.prompt: 10 (a) A Ferris wheel of radius 20 m rotates with an angular speed of 0.2 rad/sec. Construct its position vector \(\mathbf{r}(t)\).
blocks.explanation:
Uniform circular motion: the passenger's angle grows at 0.2 rad every second.
Find: a position vector for a passenger on the rim.
Plan: centre at the origin, passenger at \((20, 0)\) at \(t = 0\), turning anticlockwise; angle \(= \omega t\).
steps:
Given: \(R = 20\) m, \(\omega = 0.2\) rad/s.
To find: \(\mathbf{r}(t)\).
Method: a point on a circle of radius \(R\) at angle \(\theta\) is \((R\cos\theta, R\sin\theta)\); here \(\theta = \omega t\).

Choice of axes
The book does not fix the axes, so we take the centre of the wheel as the origin and suppose the passenger is at \((20, 0)\) at \(t = 0\) and the wheel turns anticlockwise.
Why: any choice is allowed; this one gives the simplest formula (the form used in Question 9).

Position vector
\[\theta = \omega t = 0.2t\]
\[\mathbf{r}(t) = 20\cos(0.2t)\,\hat{i}\]
\[\quad + 20\sin(0.2t)\,\hat{j}\]
Why: in \(t\) seconds the wheel turns through \(0.2t\) radians.

Check
\(|\mathbf{r}(t)| = \sqrt{400\cos^{2}(0.2t) + 400\sin^{2}(0.2t)} = 20\): the passenger always stays on the rim.
blocks.final_answer: \(\mathbf{r}(t) = 20\cos(0.2t)\,\hat{i} + 20\sin(0.2t)\,\hat{j}\) metres (centre at the origin, passenger at \((20, 0)\) when \(t = 0\), turning anticlockwise).

blocks.prompt: 10 (b) A Ferris wheel of radius 20 m rotates with an angular speed of 0.2 rad/sec. Find the passenger's velocity at \(t = 10\) sec.
blocks.explanation:
Velocity is the derivative of the position vector from part (a).
Find: \(\mathbf{v}(10)\).
Plan: differentiate with the chain rule, put \(t = 10\) (angle 2 radians).
steps:
Velocity
\[\mathbf{v}(t) = -20(0.2)\sin(0.2t)\,\hat{i}\]
\[\quad + 20(0.2)\cos(0.2t)\,\hat{j}\]
\[= -4\sin(0.2t)\,\hat{i} + 4\cos(0.2t)\,\hat{j}\]
Why: chain rule; the inner derivative is 0.2.

Meaning and check
\[|\mathbf{v}| = \sqrt{16\sin^{2}2 + 16\cos^{2}2} = 4 \text{ m/s}\]
This equals \(R\omega = 20 \times 0.2 = 4\). At \(t = 10\) the passenger is at about \((-8.32, 18.19)\), near the top-left of the wheel, moving to the left and downward.

answer_figure.alt: Circle of radius 20 centred at the origin. The passenger P at t = 10 s is at about (-8.32, 18.19) in the upper left; a red arrow shows the velocity pointing left and down along the tangent, and a green arrow points from P towards the centre.
answer_figure.caption: Ferris wheel r(t) = 20 cos(0.2t) i + 20 sin(0.2t) j: at t = 10 s the velocity is tangent and the acceleration points to the centre (arrows scaled; original drawing)

blocks.prompt: 10 (c) A Ferris wheel of radius 20 m rotates with an angular speed of 0.2 rad/sec. Show that the acceleration is centripetal (toward the center).
blocks.explanation:
'Centripetal' means pointing to the centre; with the centre at the origin, that is the direction of \(-\mathbf{r}\).
Find \(\mathbf{a}(t)\) and compare it with \(\mathbf{r}(t)\).
Plan: differentiate \(\mathbf{v}(t)\) and write \(\mathbf{a}\) as a negative multiple of \(\mathbf{r}\).
steps:
Given: \(\mathbf{v}(t) = -4\sin(0.2t)\,\hat{i} + 4\cos(0.2t)\,\hat{j}\).
To prove: \(\mathbf{a}(t)\) points to the centre for every \(t\).
Method: as in Question 7(c).

Direction
\(\mathbf{r}(t)\) points from the centre to the passenger, so the negative multiple \(-0.04\,\mathbf{r}(t)\) points from the passenger to the centre at every instant: the acceleration is centripetal.
Why: a negative multiple reverses the direction.

Size and check
\[|\mathbf{a}| = 0.04 \times 20 = 0.8 \text{ m/s}^{2}\]
\[\dfrac{v^{2}}{R} = \dfrac{4^{2}}{20} = 0.8 \text{ m/s}^{2}\]
The two agree.
blocks.final_answer: Hence proved: \(\mathbf{a}(t) = -0.04\,\mathbf{r}(t)\), which points from the passenger to the centre, so the acceleration is centripetal; \(|\mathbf{a}| = 0.8\) m/s\(^{2}\).

blocks.text: The textbook prints no answers for Exercise 11.3 (it prints no answers for any exercise of Unit 11). Every answer on this page is ours: worked out step by step, checked independently with a computer algebra system (sympy) and compared with a solution book. Angles such as \(t = \frac{\pi}{2}\) are in radians.
